o: Two characters conflict if equal or alphabetically adjacent. We may rewrite any character and want the minimum edits so no adjacent pair conflicts. Greedy works: scan left to right; whenever word[i] conflicts with the (possibly already fixed) word[i-1], edit word[i] to a letter that conflicts with neither neighbor and count one edit. "aaaaa" needs 2 (positions 1 and 3 changed), matching the example.
k: Editing word[i] can simultaneously resolve the pair (i-1,i) and prevent (i,i+1) — greedy left-to-right is optimal.
When editing, choose a replacement avoiding both neighbors; a valid letter always exists among 26 options.

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy scan with safe replacement
a.i: Process i from 1 to n-1. If |word[i]-word[i-1]| <= 1, increment the answer and replace word[i] with any letter at distance > 1 from both word[i-1] and word[i+1]. Any later conflict is handled identically, and one edit per conflict position is a lower bound the greedy achieves.
s: Convert the string to a mutable list.
For each i >= 1, test conflict with the previous character.
On conflict, count an edit and pick the first letter valid against both neighbors.
a.t: O(26n) — linear scan with a constant-time letter search per edit.
a.sp: O(n) for the mutable copy (O(1) in languages with in-place strings).

a.i: Since editing position i fixes both (i-1,i) and (i,i+1), the answer equals the number of disjoint conflicting pairs: scan and whenever word[i] conflicts with word[i-1], count 1 and skip ahead by 2. This avoids choosing replacements entirely and is provably equivalent to the greedy.
s: Scan i from 1; if word[i] almost-equals word[i-1], increment answer and jump i by 2.

w: Present the skip-by-2 version as the punchline — it makes correctness obvious (each edit resolves at most one new conflicting pair, and matched pairs are independent). Pitfall: 'almost-equal' includes equality, so identical letters conflict too.
